level-1.title: What a bank does with your money

story.title: The mice that ate the iron
text: A trader had a heavy iron balance. He was going away, so he left it with a friend to keep safe.
When he came back, he asked for it. The friend said, "I am very sorry. Mice ate the iron."
The trader said nothing. Later he took the friend's son to the river, and came back alone.
"Where is my son?" cried the friend. "A hawk carried him away," said the trader. "That is impossible!" said the friend. "If mice can eat iron," said the trader, "a hawk can carry a boy."
story.moral: The friend kept no record, so it came down to who was believed. A bank writes down what is yours, in your name, so nobody has to be believed.

summary: A bank is a safe place to keep money. Safer than a pocket, a box, or under a bed.
Money in a pocket can be lost or taken. Money in a bank cannot.
The bank writes down every rupee that is yours. That written record is your account.
You can put money in and take money out when you need it. It stays yours the whole time.
The bank pays you a small extra amount for keeping your money there. A box pays you nothing.

options.label: Your friend's - a bank keeps a written record, a school bag does not
Yours - banks can lose records too

options.label: You can withdraw it - it was always yours, the bank was only keeping it

image.alt: A box beside a bank, with a small plant growing from the bank

options.label: You do - the bank pays a little extra for keeping your money there

level-2.title: Opening an account in your own name

story.title: The mice that ate the iron
text: A trader was leaving on a long journey and did not want to carry his iron balance - a heavy, valuable thing. He left it with a friend for safekeeping. No paper was signed, because they were friends.
When he returned and asked for it, the friend was full of regret. "Mice ate the iron," he said.
The trader accepted this without argument. A few days later he offered to take the friend's son down to the river, and came back without him.

When the friend demanded to know where the boy was, the trader said a hawk had carried him off. The friend shouted that no hawk could lift a boy. "In a town where mice eat iron," the trader replied, "a hawk can certainly carry a child."
story.moral: Both stories were absurd, and neither man could prove anything - there was no record, so it came down to whose word won. A bank account replaces a promise with an entry: the amount, the date, and whose name it is under.

summary: You can hold a bank account in your own name from the age of 10. An adult helps manage it until you are 18, but the account is yours.
A basic account needs no minimum balance. You can open it with nothing in it, and leaving it empty costs you nothing.
It comes with a debit card, so you can pay and withdraw without asking anyone for permission.
The account is where your own money lives - pocket money, gifts, and anything you earn later.
Check the exact rules at the bank before you go. Schemes change, and different banks ask for different papers.

level-3.title: The account as a foundation, and your right to one

story.title: The mice that ate the iron
text: Before a long journey a trader deposited his iron balance with a friend. It was heavy and valuable and there was nowhere safer he could think of. Nothing was written down.
On his return the friend explained, with apparent sorrow, that mice had eaten the iron.
The trader did not argue the point. Instead he took the man's son out to the river, returned alone, and reported that a hawk had carried the boy away.
The friend erupted - and in doing so had to argue that some things are simply not possible. Which was precisely the trader's point, made back to him.
story.moral: Neither party could prove anything, so the outcome depended on leverage rather than fact. What a bank sells is not a safe: it is a record, held by a third party, in your own name, that neither of you can quietly edit. That is why the account has to be in the name of the person the money belongs to.

summary: The account is not the goal. It is what everything else plugs into - a salary, a scholarship, a pension, a fund held in your name.
Money you are owed is normally paid only into an account in your own name. Without one, somebody else receives it on your behalf.
That is the real argument for holding your own: it is the difference between managing your money and being managed.
A savings account pays roughly 4% a year while prices rise around 6%. Money parked there quietly loses ground - an account is for safety and access, not for growth.
The law is behind you when you open one. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 requires service providers, banks included, to make their services accessible.
A bank that refuses you, or insists a hearing relative speaks for you, is not following the rules. Ask for the branch manager, then the bank's grievance officer, then the RBI ombudsman.

questions.prompt: A savings account pays 4% a year. Prices rise 6% a year. You keep ₹2000 in the account for one year, adding nothing. Roughly how much buying power do you lose?

image.alt: Two arrows, one rising faster than the other, beside two thousand rupees

options.label: About ₹40 of buying power
About ₹120 of buying power gained
No change at all

questions.hint: Find the gap between the two percentages, then apply it to ₹2000.

questions.prompt: A bank clerk refuses to open your account because you are Deaf. You calmly object but they still refuse. What is the correct next step, in order?

image.alt: A law book beside a bank counter with three escalation steps

options.label: Ask for the branch manager; if that fails, the bank's grievance officer; if that fails, the RBI ombudsman
Go straight to the RBI ombudsman first
Accept the refusal, since the clerk has final say

questions.hint: The lesson gives three steps, and they have a specific order - start local, escalate outward.

questions.prompt: Your grandmother is owed a monthly government pension, but she has no bank account of her own - it is currently paid into her son's account. What risk does this create?

image.alt: A pension payment landing in someone else's account

options.label: She does not fully control money that is legally hers, the same problem as with a scholarship paid to someone else
No risk - pensions are always safe wherever they land
This is required by law and cannot be changed

questions.hint: Apply the same reasoning used earlier about scholarships and funds needing your own name.
